findings.title: The proposed actor-owned staging-upload boundary has no enforceable ownership artifact

sourceEvidence.explanation: The existing upload result is a public Blob URL derived from a timestamp and sanitized client filename; no actor binding or capability is persisted or returned.
Fallbacks return a public local path or transferable data URL, likewise without an actor-bound staging record or verifiable attachment capability.
The supplied schema has final attachment records but no staging-upload ownership model, and the revised package forbids schema changes.

findings.impact: The design requires a staging upload to belong to actor.id and requires later attachment to enforce the teaching or owned-submission boundary, but it defines no persisted owner record, signed actor-bound capability, or equivalent verifier. Possession of a returned URL can therefore be replayed by another authenticated actor at a later attachment endpoint, so the stated ownership boundary cannot be implemented from this contract.
findings.recommendation: Revise the contract to specify an enforceable handoff artifact and its lifecycle. For example, define a server-side staging record keyed to actor.id and institute, or a short-lived integrity-protected capability bound to actor, object identity, size/type, and intended use; require attachment operations to consume and verify it. If schema changes remain forbidden, explicitly define a reviewed storage/provider mechanism that supplies equivalent binding, expiry, and single-use/revocation semantics.

findings.title: Workspace event policy does not define authorization for reading shared course events

sourceEvidence.explanation: The baseline reads one event or all events by institute only, including the linked course title; creator ownership and course membership are not applied.
A caller-supplied courseId is stored and its course title returned, showing that course linkage affects protected data.
CalendarEvent represents both creator-owned and optionally course-linked records, so read authorization must distinguish personal and shared-course visibility.

findings.impact: The revised WORKSPACE relation defines ownership for personal events and instructor/Admin authority for management of shared teaching schedules, but it never states which students or other normal actors may read shared course events. Implementers could retain institute-wide disclosure, hide legitimate enrolled-course schedules, or apply creator-only access inconsistently. The exact GET authorization boundary is therefore not implementation-ready.
findings.recommendation: Add an operation-specific GET rule: personal events require creatorId=actor.id; course-linked events require an explicitly selected persisted visibility rule, such as approved enrollment, assigned instructor, or Admin authority, with course.instituteId matching the actor/institute. Define list query constraints and single-record safe-404 behavior from the same predicate. Keep POST/PATCH/DELETE management rules separately explicit.

findings.title: Course-linked personal tasks lack a persisted course-relationship rule

sourceEvidence.explanation: POST accepts courseId and immediately returns the linked course title without resolving the actor's enrollment, assignment, or Admin authority.
PATCH verifies ownership of the task but permits replacement courseId and returns the linked course title without a course-access predicate.
GET includes linked course title for owned tasks, making unauthorized course linkage a disclosure path.
TaskItem.courseId is an optional unrestricted relation; the schema itself does not enforce actor access to the referenced course.

findings.impact: The revised WORKSPACE policy says only that a linked Course matches the institute, while personal task authority is creator ownership. Same-institute actors could therefore link their own task to a course they are not enrolled in or assigned to and obtain course metadata. The design's general requirement for persisted relationship authorization is not expressed for this operation.
findings.recommendation: Specify that any non-null TaskItem.courseId must resolve to an actual same-institute course for which the actor has COURSE_READ authority: approved enrollment, instructor assignment, or Admin authority. Apply that predicate before create/update and when returning linked course data; use a uniform safe 404 for a foreign or unauthorized course.

implementationRisks.title: Baseline account routes do not enforce the revised role ceilings and relationship rules

sourceEvidence.explanation: Both methods accept any authenticated session; no explicit recognized-role check denies SUPER_USER or UNKNOWN before reads, parsing, or writes.
The route parses and updates preferences for any authenticated session and returns the full updated user object without a normal-role ceiling.

The target user and extensive profile relations are read before authorization; authorization checks only institute equality and does not require self, Admin, or a persisted shared-course relationship.

implementationRisks.impact: Until implemented, SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN actors can reach unsupported account routes, and arbitrary same-institute profiles can be disclosed before the revised PROFILE_READ relationship is enforced.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Implement the canonical actor resolver and explicit normal-role guard before protected parsing or reads. For third-party profiles, constrain the initial query to self, Admin, or a persisted shared-course relationship and return a uniform safe 404 for unauthorized targets.

implementationRisks.title: Baseline study-session routes do not enforce student role or persisted course/item relationships

sourceEvidence.explanation: POST accepts caller courseId and syllabusItemId, creates the log, then grants EXP and checks badges without verifying STUDENT role, approved enrollment, same institute, or that the item belongs to the course.
GET filters actor-owned logs by caller courseId but does not enforce current enrollment or institute relationship.

implementationRisks.impact: An authenticated unsupported role, including SUPER_USER, can invoke study effects, while a student can bind logs and gamification effects to unauthorized or mismatched course resources.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Before parsing protected inputs or effects, enforce recognized STUDENT role. Resolve non-null course and syllabus item through one approved enrollment and same-institute parent chain, reject mismatches with safe 404, and only then create the log or trigger gamification.

implementationRisks.title: Baseline todo route lacks an explicit student-role and home-institute guard

sourceEvidence.explanation: The route accepts any authenticated session, resolves a caller-selected institute, and enumerates that actor's enrollments without verifying STUDENT role or matching the institute to the actor's persisted home institute.
An unauthorized course filter returns 403 rather than the revised uniform safe 404, and response construction exposes course and instructor metadata.

implementationRisks.impact: SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN or other non-student actors are not denied at entry, and the error contract can reveal whether a requested course falls outside the actor's enrollment set.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Apply canonical authentication, recognized STUDENT role, and persisted home-institute equality before institute/course reads. Constrain course selection through approved enrollment and return the required uniform safe 404 for unavailable or unauthorized course targets.

implementationRisks.title: Baseline upload route permits unsupported roles and publishes unbound content

sourceEvidence.explanation: Only session presence is checked before multipart parsing; there is no recognized-role ceiling or explicit SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN denial.
Files are published as public Blob URLs, public filesystem paths, or transferable data URLs without actor ownership metadata.

implementationRisks.impact: Until the revised design and the separate handoff contract are implemented, unsupported actors can consume storage and publish content, and subsequent attachment operations cannot prove ownership of returned upload references.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Deny SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN before multipart parsing, validate a recognized normal role, and implement the revised actor-bound staging mechanism before returning an attachable reference.

implementationRisks.title: Baseline workspace handlers do not explicitly deny SUPER_USER or UNKNOWN

sourceEvidence.explanation: All methods rely on requireWorkspaceSession and contain no local recognized-role or explicit SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN denial; event reads and mutations also use institute scope rather than the revised ownership/course authority.
Ownership predicates exist for reads and mutations, but no method locally enforces the revised normal-role ceiling before protected parsing/read/write.
Ownership predicates exist for task records, but no explicit normal-role ceiling is present and courseId is accepted without relationship validation.

implementationRisks.impact: If the unsupplied shared helper authenticates without enforcing the new role contract, SUPER_USER and UNKNOWN can use legacy workspace features. Events additionally expose and mutate institute-wide records, while task course links lack resource authorization.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Implement a canonical WORKSPACE guard at every method entry that validates active authentication, recognized normal role, and persisted institute before parsing or database access. Then apply operation-specific ownership and linked-course predicates, including the revised event-read and task-link rules.

implementationRisks.title: Canonical role handling required by the design is not implemented in supplied shared policy

sourceEvidence.explanation: The baseline role normalizer maps every unrecognized value, including SUPER_USER and malformed roles, to STUDENT.
Shared guards consume the unsafe normalizer; requirePermission may grant a non-Admin unknown/SUPER_USER actor based on stored permissions, contrary to the hard legacy ceiling.
Session validation establishes active identity but does not implement the revised explicit role classification or operation capability.

implementationRisks.impact: Reusing baseline normalization or permission helpers during implementation can silently confer STUDENT behavior or stored permission capabilities on SUPER_USER/UNKNOWN, defeating route-specific denial rules across this subset.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Introduce and consistently use a fail-closed role classifier that returns explicit UNKNOWN and SUPER_USER values. Keep the managed-role normalizer limited to validated ADMIN/INSTRUCTOR/STUDENT inputs, and prohibit persisted permissions from overriding the SUPER_USER legacy ceiling.

implementationRisks.title: Public leaderboard baseline may disclose users who have not opted in

sourceEvidence.explanation: The public query filters role, activity, and active status but does not filter GamificationProfile.publicLeaderboardOptIn.
The model includes publicLeaderboardOptIn, demonstrating an existing persisted public-disclosure control.

implementationRisks.impact: Because U-01 preserves this endpoint as anonymous and unchanged, the current implementation can publish a student's identity or pseudonymous stable identifier despite an opt-out value. This is a known baseline exposure, not a defect introduced by the revised Super User design.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Track this under the existing public-leaderboard privacy contract and remediate only through the separately authorized U-01/public scope; do not add Super User-specific optional authentication behavior here.

implementationRisks.title: Production metadata trust and revocation operations remain unassigned

sourceEvidence.explanation: The supplied document explicitly leaves the trusted academic/privacy approver, manifest maintainer/release reviewer, production dataset ID/fingerprint and attestation procedure, expiry lifetime, and revocation owner/runbook as required human or operator assignments.

implementationRisks.impact: Deny-by-default permits safe non-deployment, but trustworthy production disclosure cannot begin until accountable identities, the production dataset binding, expiry policy, and publication/revocation procedure exist. No reviewer may invent those assignments.
implementationRisks.recommendation: Before production deployment, obtain and record the named governance assignments and dataset attestation procedure through the authorized human process. Continue withholding all oversight results while any required assignment or valid manifest is absent.

coverage.assessment: Reviewed both assigned methods against OWN, canonical actor selection, explicit normal-role ceiling, self binding, denial ordering, and response effects. The revised rule is coherent, but baseline implementation lacks the role ceiling.

Reviewed the assigned anonymous GET as the unchanged U-01 PUBLIC exception. No Super User-specific denial should be added; existing opt-in exposure remains an implementation risk outside revised Super User behavior.
Reviewed PATCH against OWN and exact basic-account support. Design correctly excludes SUPER_USER, while baseline accepts any authenticated actor and returns an overbroad user record.

Reviewed both methods against MATERIAL, STUDENT-only capability, actor ownership, approved enrollment, institute binding, course/item parent consistency, and gamification-effect ordering. Baseline controls are not remediated.

Reviewed GET against STUDENT_WORK, route institute, approved enrollment, course filter, child-query binding, and safe denial. The revised design is adequate for this operation; baseline lacks explicit role/home-institute enforcement.

Reviewed POST against UPLOAD role, institute, actor ownership, pre-parse denial, storage publication, and later attachment binding. The staging-ownership handoff is not implementable from the stated design and causes REVIEW_FAIL.

Reviewed GET against PROFILE_READ self/Admin/shared-course relationship, institute scope, pre-read authorization, and Super User denial. The revised relationship rule is adequate, but the baseline reads before applying only an institute check.

Reviewed all four methods against WORKSPACE actor, institute, personal ownership, shared-course management, denial ordering, linked parent binding, and effects. The design omits the shared-course event read predicate and therefore is not implementation-ready.

Reviewed all four methods against WORKSPACE normal-role ceiling, actor creator ownership, institute scope, safe 404 behavior, and mutation ordering. The design is coherent for personal notes; baseline explicit role enforcement remains pending.

Reviewed all four methods against WORKSPACE ownership, institute scope, optional course linkage, denial ordering, and returned course data. The design fails to require a persisted relationship to a linked course for GET/POST/PATCH.

limitations: This was a document-only pre-implementation design review. Per instruction, no tools, filesystem reads, commands, tests, database operations, external requests, source changes, or approvals were performed.

The sanitized body of apps/web/src/app/api/workspace/_shared was not supplied. Consequently, the current behavior of requireWorkspaceSession and getQueryId could not be independently inspected; route-local absence of revised role checks is reported as an implementation risk rather than assuming helper behavior.
transactionEvidence is null. Transaction runtime behavior was not evaluated as implemented evidence, and none is required for this assigned legacy-route subset's design verdict.
No acceptance-criteria catalog with separate AC numbers was supplied. affectedAC therefore uses the exact assigned operation-matrix IDs, which are the request-bound criteria available in the packet.

Line-addressable content for 008-revised-super-user-architecture.md was supplied as one unnumbered document value; evidence from that document is therefore cited at line 1 rather than fabricating line ranges.
No product validation, formal harness gate, implementation approval, or remediation claim is made. Every finding and implementation risk remains unresolved.
